But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him."<sup>27</sup>Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother."<sup>28</sup>And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
3.overview:
Three verses open the chapter that anybody reading quickly would take as favourable, and each has something in it the rest of the history comes back for. A marriage alliance with Egypt — a political triumph, since Egypt did not give daughters to foreign kings — and the law had told Israel's king not to send people back there and not to take many wives lest his heart turn away, in consecutive clauses. Chapter 11 names the daughter of Pharaoh first in the list of the women who turned him.

Then the finest compliment in the book: Solomon loved the LORD, which this writer says of nobody else. And then his needle: only he sacrificed at the high places — the word he will attach to almost every good reign for the rest of both books.

At Gibeon God asks him what he wants, with no terms and no hint of a right answer, which is why the request is a photograph of the heart taken from the inside. He asks for lev shomea, a hearing heart — not a clever mind, not a quick answer, but a deciding faculty that takes things in before it rules, which is exactly what his father had stopped having. And God names the three things he did not ask for: long life, riches, the life of his enemies — the three things every king in that world wanted, and Solomon had reason to want the third. Two of them are given anyway, outright. Long life is the one with an if attached.

And then, straight after a thousand burnt offerings and an appearance of God, two prostitutes are standing in a room. No husbands, no witnesses, no standing, nothing to offer — the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person. He cannot detect the liar, so he makes a situation in which love has to reveal itself, because love acts against its own interest and a false claim never does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Only at the High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem (v. 1). The people were sacrificing at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD (v. 2). Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The first fact recorded about the reign after the executions is a foreign marriage, and to Egypt of all places. The law had told Israel's king not to send people back there and not to take many wives lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17). The writer states it and adds nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 3 has the needle in it: Solomon loved the LORD — which is said of nobody else in Kings — only he sacrificed at the high places. The word only is the verdict this writer keeps attaching to good kings, and the high places are the thing that will still be standing at the end of both books.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem. The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD. Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem.'

The first thing recorded about the reign, once the executions are over, is a wedding to Egypt.

Politically it is a triumph and everybody at the time would have read it that way. Egypt did not give daughters to foreign kings; the Amarna correspondence has a pharaoh saying flatly that a daughter of Egypt is given to nobody. That Solomon got one is a measure of how large Israel had suddenly become.

And the writer records it in the flattest possible sentence and moves on.

Hold two things against it.

The first is the law about Israel's kings, which this history keeps quietly measuring people by. Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses... And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17). Egypt and wives, in consecutive clauses, and this verse has both.

And there is the older command about marrying into the nations of the land: you shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:3-4). The reason given in the law is never about race. It is about what happens to worship in a household.

The second is what chapter 11 says happened. Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh... For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods (11:1-4).

The daughter of Pharaoh is named first in that list, and she arrives here, in verse 1, before the temple is built and before Gibeon.

This writer does not editorialise. He plants and waits, and this is a plant.

'The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.'

The high places are open-air sanctuaries on hilltops, and they are going to be the running problem of both books.

And the writer gives the excuse himself, which is unusually generous of him: because no house had yet been built. There is no temple yet. The tabernacle is at Gibeon and the ark is in a tent in Jerusalem, and worship is scattered.

'Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.'

Now read that verse twice, because it holds the whole reign in one line.

Solomon loved the LORD. That is a remarkable thing to say and the writer of Kings says it of nobody else. Not of Asa, not of Jehoshaphat, not of Hezekiah or Josiah, who get his highest marks. Solomon alone is said to have loved God.

Then: only.

That little word is this writer's needle and he uses it for the rest of both books. King after king will be told he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, only the high places were not taken away, only the people still sacrificed there. It is the standing qualification on almost every good reign in the history.

Here it appears for the first time, and it is attached to Solomon on the page before he asks for wisdom.

So the chapter opens with three verses that anybody reading quickly would take as a favourable introduction: a magnificent alliance, a plausible explanation for irregular worship, and the finest compliment in the book. And each of the three has something in it that the rest of the history will come back for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Gibeon Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings, and God appears to him in a dream by night: ask what I shall give you (vv. 4-5). He answers with what God did for David, and then: I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in... Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people? (vv. 7-9). It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this (v. 10), and God names what he did not ask for — long life, riches, the life of his enemies — and gives him a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you, and riches and honour as well (vv. 11-13). And one condition: and if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days (v. 14). He wakes, and it was a dream (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The Hebrew of verse 9 is a hearing heart. Not a clever mind and not a large one — a heart that listens, which is what a judge needs before anything else, and what his father stopped having.
verseByVerse.examples: And the gifts are not given on the same terms. Wisdom and riches are given outright; length of days has an if attached to it. Chapter 11 is where that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you." And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day. And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in. And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude. Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?" It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this. And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right, behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you. I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days. And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days." And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings upon that altar.'

Gibeon is where the tabernacle was — the tent Moses made, with the bronze altar, still standing there (2 Chron. 1:3-5). So this is not one of the irregular hilltop shrines; it is the national sanctuary, at the town whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty and were spared for the sake of an oath.

A thousand burnt offerings is an enormous act. A burnt offering is the sacrifice that is entirely consumed, with nothing kept back for the worshipper to eat.

'At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you."'

God asks him what he wants.

It is the only time in Scripture the question is put quite like this, to one person, open. There are no terms attached and no hint of what would be a good answer. Ask what I shall give you.

Any reader knows immediately that this is a test, and the reason should be clear. Nothing reveals a person like what they ask for when they can have anything. The request is a photograph of the heart taken from the inside.

'And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day."'

He does not begin with a request. He begins with what God has already done, and the word he uses twice is hesed — the covenant love that keeps its promises after the reasons for keeping them are gone.

And note his description of his father: he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart.

A reader who has just finished 2 Samuel may find that hard to take, and it needs saying plainly that it is a son's account and not a full one. It is also not false. David never served another god, and repented when he was confronted, and the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 was grounded in God's character rather than his. Solomon is describing the shape of a life, not auditing it.

'"And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in."'

Here is the beginning of the answer, and it is an admission.

I am but a little child. He is not literally a child; he is a grown man who has just executed four people and married a princess of Egypt. Josephus says he was fourteen, and most estimates put him around twenty. Whatever the figure, the phrase is a confession of competence, not of age.

I do not know how to go out or come in. That is a soldier's idiom for leading an army out and bringing it home, and it is what the elders said about David when they made him king — it was you who led out and brought in Israel (2 Sam. 5:2).

Solomon is saying: I cannot do what my father did.

'"And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude."'

Note whose people they are. Your people whom you have chosen. He has been on the throne for a matter of months and he already knows that the nation is not his.

And there is a small barb in too many to be numbered, since the last thing his father did before the plague was count them.

'"Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?"'

Here is the request, and it is the sentence the first half of this book turns on.

Take the Hebrew exactly. What he asks for is lev shomea — a hearing heart.

Not a clever mind. Not a large memory or a quick answer or the ability to out-argue people. A heart that listens.

In Hebrew the heart is not the seat of the feelings as it is in English; it is where a person thinks and decides. So a hearing heart is a deciding faculty that takes things in before it rules — and it is precisely what a judge needs and precisely what his father had stopped having. Two men came to David with stories in 2 Samuel: he heard one side from Ziba and handed over an estate in a sentence, and then heard the other side and split the land rather than admit he had judged carelessly.

And note the purpose he attaches to it: to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil. The request is not for his own benefit. It is a tool for a job, and the job is other people.

The last clause is the honest one. Who is able to govern this your great people? That is not modesty; it is a real question with an implied answer, which is nobody. He has looked at what is in front of him and concluded that it cannot be done, and asked for the one thing that would let him try.

'It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.'

'And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right,"'

God names what he did not ask for, which is the most revealing verse in the chapter.

Three things, and they are the three things every king in the ancient world wanted, in order.

Long life. To stay on the throne and not be killed on it.

Riches. The measure of a reign, then as now.

The life of your enemies. To have the men who threaten you dead.

Solomon had reason to want the third. He had spent his first year dealing with a brother, a general, a priest and a Benjaminite, and there were more where they came from.

He asked for none of the three.

Here is what makes this passage useful rather than merely admirable. God did not tell him the right answer beforehand. There was no hint, no list of approved requests, no indication that asking for wealth would disappoint. The question was genuinely open, and what came out of him was a hearing heart to do a job for somebody else's people.

That is why it pleased God. Not the eloquence of it — the fact that when a man could have had anything at all, this is what was in him.

'"behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you."'

He gets exactly what he asked for, and more of it than anyone before or since.

'"I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days."'

Then two of the three things he did not ask for, given anyway.

There is a principle here that the Lord Jesus states directly, and he may well have this chapter in view: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. 6:33). The order is the whole of it. Solomon did not get riches because he declined to want them as a technique; he got them because the man who asks for a hearing heart is the man it is safe to give them to.

Whether it stayed safe is chapter 10's question.

'"And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days."'

Now read the difference between this verse and the two before it, because it is deliberate and it is the hinge of Solomon's whole life.

Wisdom: behold, I give you. Riches and honour: I give you also. Given. No condition, no requirement, no test.

Long life: if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days.

The one thing he did not receive outright is the one thing hedged with an if, and the condition is conduct, and the standard named is his father.

Keep it, because the writer will come back for it. In chapter 11 God says to Solomon: since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you (11:11). The gifts were never withdrawn — he died the wisest and richest man in the world — and the conditional promise was.

'And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.'

He wakes up, and the writer says plainly what it was.

Behold, it was a dream. That is not scepticism; the writer has just told us God appeared to him. It is precision. Solomon did not have a vision he could point to or a stone he could show anybody. He woke up in the dark at Gibeon with a conversation in his head.

Look at what he does with it.

He goes to Jerusalem, and he stands in front of the ark, and he offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, and he throws a feast for his whole household.

Burnt offerings are wholly consumed; peace offerings are eaten. So there is a sacrifice that keeps nothing back, and then a meal, and everybody who works for him is at it.

A man is given the greatest promise of his life in his sleep, and the first thing he does when he wakes is go and worship where the ark is, and then feed his servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–28 — Give Her the Living Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two prostitutes come to the king. They live in one house; both bore sons three days apart; one child died in the night, and each says the living one is hers (vv. 16-22). The king states the deadlock — the one says, "This is my son that is alive"... and the other says, "No; but your son is dead" — and calls for a sword: divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other (vv. 23-25). Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." (v. 26). The king gives the child to the first — she is his mother (v. 27). And all Israel hears, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Note who gets a hearing. Two prostitutes with no husbands, no witnesses, no standing and nothing to offer, in a case turning entirely on one woman's word against another's — and it goes to the king in person. That is justice and equity to all his people (2 Sam. 8:15) actually operating.
verseByVerse.examples: And he does not detect a liar. He makes a situation in which love has to show itself, because love will act against its own interest and a false claim will not. The real mother gives up the child to keep him alive; the other says let him be neither mine nor yours.

verseByVerse.quote: Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him. The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house. Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house. And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him. And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast. When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne." But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king. Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'" And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king. And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other." Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother." And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.'

Now watch what the writer does, because the placement of this story is the argument.

The previous paragraph had a thousand burnt offerings, an appearance of God, and a promise that no king would compare with him. The very next sentence is two prostitutes standing in a room.

Consider what these women are and are not. They have no husbands and no male relative to speak for them. They have no standing in any court. They have nothing to give and nobody to bribe, and their profession puts them at the bottom of the society. The whole case rests on one woman's word against another's, in a house with no other adults in it, and there are no witnesses of any kind.

It is the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person.

That is the point. The wisdom that was promised in a dream at Gibeon shows up first in a hearing that nobody powerful cared about, and the writer put the two paragraphs next to each other so that the reader would see it.

And it is the sentence that summarised David's reign at its best, operating: David administered justice and equity to all his people (2 Sam. 8:15). All was always the test, because the courts of that world were judged by how they treated the people nobody had to be fair to.

'The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house."'

'"Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house."'

She states the evidential problem herself: there was no one else with us in the house. No witnesses. She knows it, and says it, and comes anyway.

'"And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him."'

'"And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast."'

'"When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne."'

There is the detail that makes the story real: when I looked at him closely in the morning.

She woke to feed a baby and the baby was dead, and in the half-light she did not know at first. It took looking properly.

'But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king.'

Two women shouting the same two sentences at each other in front of a throne.

'Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'"'

He states the deadlock back to them, exactly, and that is the first thing a hearing heart does.

He has listened closely enough to reproduce both positions without favouring either, and he has established out loud that there is nothing to choose between them on the evidence. No amount of further questioning will settle it.

'And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king.'

'And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other."'

The room stops.

It has to be said that this is a terrible thing to say in front of a woman holding a baby, and the writer does not soften it. A sword is fetched. The order is given in plain words. Neither woman knows it is a test, and one of them is about to watch her child be cut in half.

Whether Solomon would have gone through with it is not a question the text raises, and the answer is obviously not. But she does not know that.

Now see what he has actually done, because it is not a trick and it is not cleverness for its own sake.

He could not tell which woman was lying. Nobody could; there was no evidence and no witness. So he stopped trying to detect a liar and made a situation in which love would have to show itself.

The insight underneath it is this: love acts against its own interest, and a false claim never does. A woman who wants a baby will not give it up. A woman who loves a baby will give up anything, including the baby, to keep him alive.

So the sword does not test their honesty. It tests what each of them wants more — the child, or winning.

'Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death."'

There it is.

Take the narrator's clause first, because he tells us the reason before he gives us her words: because her heart yearned for her son.

The Hebrew verb is physical. It is about the inward parts turning over — the churn a person feels in the body when someone they love is in danger. It is the word used of Joseph, when he saw his brother Benjamin and had to leave the room because his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep (Gen. 43:30).

That is what is happening in her while she speaks.

Now what she says. Give her the living child.

She loses. That is the whole point and it should not be hurried past. In order to keep her son alive she has to hand him to the woman who stole him, and go home without him, and live the rest of her life knowing where he is and unable to say a word about it.

She does it in one sentence, and the second half of the sentence is the only thing she cares about: and by no means put him to death.

'But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him."'

The other one says the coldest sentence in the chapter.

He shall be neither mine nor yours.

Notice what she is actually choosing. She is not choosing the child; she has already lost that option, because the king has ruled that neither gets him whole. She is choosing that the other woman shall not have him either.

That is what a grief with nothing underneath it turns into when it is refused. She lost her own son in the night and lay there and swapped the bodies, and what she wants now is not a baby. It is that the woman across the room should not be happy.

Anybody who has watched a bitter dispute go past the point where either party can gain anything has seen this exact sentence. Neither mine nor yours. If I cannot have it, destroy it.

'Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother."'

He gives the verdict in her own words. By no means put him to death is what she said, and he says it back, and then three words: she is his mother.

'And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.'

The last verse is careful about what it is praising.

Not that the king was clever. They perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.

The wisdom is God's, given at Gibeon a page ago, and it is identified by what it produced: a right verdict in a case nobody could have decided, for a woman with no standing whatever.

That is what Solomon asked for. He wanted a hearing heart to discern between good and evil so that he could govern God's people, and the first thing it did was find a baby's mother.

And there is something in the shape of it that runs further than this courtroom. A real mother gave up her claim so that her son could live. A while later, in the same city, God gave up a Son so that people with no standing and no case and nothing to offer could live — and both of them did it by surrendering the thing they had every right to keep.

3.theology:
The plant in verse 1. The first fact recorded about the reign after the executions is a wedding to Egypt, stated flatly and left there. The word only (v. 3). Solomon loved the LORD is said of no other king in Kings — not Asa, not Jehoshaphat, not Hezekiah or Josiah, who get the highest marks. And the qualification attached to him on the page before he asks for wisdom is the one this writer will attach to almost every good reign that follows: the high places were not taken away. He is generous enough to give the excuse himself in verse 2 — there was no temple yet.

An open question is a photograph of the heart (v. 5). No terms, no hint of an approved answer, no indication that asking for wealth would disappoint. Nothing reveals a person like what they ask for when they can have anything.

Two of the three, given anyway (v. 13). Whether it stayed safe is chapter 10's question.

The one gift with an if (v. 14). Read the difference deliberately: wisdom, behold, I give you; riches and honour, I give you also. Given outright, no condition. Long life: if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days, and the standard named is his father. Solomon had no vision to point to and no stone to show anybody; he woke in the dark at Gibeon with a conversation in his head. And what he does with it: goes to Jerusalem, stands before the ark, offers burnt offerings (wholly consumed) and peace offerings (eaten), and feeds his whole household.

Who gets a hearing (v. 16). The placement is the argument. A thousand burnt offerings, an appearance of God, and a promise that no king would compare with him — and the next sentence is two prostitutes standing in a room. No husbands, no male relative to speak for them, no standing in any court, nothing to give and nobody to bribe, and a case turning entirely on one woman's word against another's with no witnesses, which she states herself. The wisdom promised at Gibeon shows up first in a hearing nobody powerful cared about. That is 2 Samuel 8:15 operating, and all his people was always the test, because the courts of that world were judged by how they treated those nobody had to be fair to.

He stops trying to detect a liar (v. 25). It is a terrible thing to say in front of a woman holding a baby, and the writer does not soften it: a sword is fetched and the order is given plainly, and neither woman knows it is a test. He could not tell which was lying — nobody could — so he made a situation in which love would have to show itself. The insight underneath is that love acts against its own interest and a false claim never does. A woman who wants a baby will not give him up; a woman who loves him will give up anything, including him, to keep him alive. The sword does not test honesty. It tests what each of them wants more: the child, or winning.

Her heart yearned (v. 26). The narrator gives the reason before the words, and the verb is physical — the inward parts turning over, the churn in the body when someone you love is in danger. It is the word used of Joseph, who saw Benjamin and had to leave the room to weep (Gen. 43:30). And she loses, which is the point: to keep him alive she must hand him to the woman who stole him and go home without him and live the rest of her life knowing where he is. She does it in one sentence, and the half she cares about is the second: by no means put him to death.

Neither mine nor yours (v. 26). The coldest sentence in the chapter, and notice what she is choosing. Not the child — that option is gone, since the ruling gives him whole to nobody. She is choosing that the other woman shall not have him either. That is what a grief with nothing underneath it becomes when it is refused: she lost her own son in the night and swapped the bodies, and what she wants now is not a baby but that the woman across the room should not be happy. Anyone who has watched a bitter dispute pass the point where either side can gain has heard that sentence.

What the last verse praises (v. 28). Not that the king was clever: they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice. The wisdom is God's, given a page earlier, and it is identified by what it produced — a right verdict in a case nobody could have decided, for a woman with no standing whatever. He asked for a hearing heart to govern God's people, and the first thing it did was find a baby's mother. And there is a shape here that runs further than the courtroom: a real mother gave up her claim so that her son could live, and later, in the same city, God gave up a Son so that people with no standing and no case could live — both by surrendering what they had every right to keep.
3.examples:
Then: God appeared to a young king in his sleep and told him to ask for anything at all, with no hint of what a good answer would be — and he asked for a heart that could listen, so that he could do the job properly for people who were not his. The first case it was used on was two prostitutes and a baby, with no witnesses and nothing to decide it by.

Now: Three things. Verse 5 is the test that never stops being a test: what you would ask for if you could have anything is a photograph of you, and nobody is going to tell you the right answer beforehand. Second, what he asked for was a tool for a job, and the job was other people — which is the difference between wanting wisdom and wanting to be thought wise. And third, the sword. He could not tell who was lying, so he stopped trying and made a situation in which love had to declare itself, because love will act against its own interest and nothing else will. Know that about other people, and know it about yourself: the question is never what you claim to care about but what you will give up to keep it.

4.overview:
A cabinet list, and the reader has seen two of these before at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and 20, both times to say the kingdom was in working order. This one is longer, and the difference is the point: two secretaries where David had one, an officer over the officers, a household manager, and a minister of forced labour. This is a state rather than a court.

The name to keep is last on the list where nobody looks. Adoniram... was in charge of the forced labor — the same office, and almost certainly the same man, as the Adoram of 2 Samuel 20:24. Eight chapters from now the ten tribes stone him to death and walk out of the kingdom, and the one thing they ask Rehoboam for is that his father's yoke be lightened. The writer puts him eleventh on a list and says nothing.

And the twelve districts are not the twelve tribes. Several are named by town or region rather than tribe, cutting straight across the old inheritances — which were not administrative conveniences but allotments given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of the land promised to Abraham. A revenue map is drawn over the top of them. It is more efficient, and when the north finally walks out the slogan is about inheritance.

Then the high-water mark of the Old Testament, in Abraham's own vocabulary: as many as the sand by the sea, and borders from the Euphrates to Egypt, and every man under his vine and under his fig tree. And in the middle of it, forty thousand stalls of horses, stated as one more item of glory, against a command his father had obeyed at cost by hamstringing a captured cavalry on the field. The father cut the tendons; the son built the stables.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Officials and the Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: King Solomon was king over all Israel, and the cabinet is listed: Azariah son of Zadok the priest; two secretaries; Jehoshaphat the recorder; Benaiah over the army; Zadok and Abiathar as priests; Azariah over the officers; Zabud son of Nathan, priest and king's friend; Ahishar over the household; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor (vv. 1-6). Then twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year (v. 7), and the districts are set out one by one (vv. 8-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The list looks like David's at 2 Samuel 8 and 20, and it is not the same kind of thing. There are two secretaries where there was one, an officer over the officers, a household manager, and a minister of forced labour. This is a state rather than a court.
verseByVerse.examples: And the twelve districts are not the twelve tribes. Several are named by town or region rather than by tribe, and the old boundaries are cut across — which turns a confederation of families into a revenue map. It is efficient, and chapter 12 is what it cost.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon was king over all Israel, and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend; Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor. Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year. These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan; Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher); Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean that is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam; Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars); Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim; Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth; Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar; Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin; Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'King Solomon was king over all Israel, and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest;'

A cabinet list, and the reader has seen two of these before — at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and again at the end of 2 Samuel 20, both times to say that the kingdom was in working order.

This one is longer, and the difference is the point of the chapter.

'Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;'

'Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;'

Two secretaries where David had one. Jehoshaphat the recorder is the same man who held the post under David, which means somebody in that administration has now served two kings.

Note that Abiathar is still listed, although he was expelled to Anathoth in chapter 2. The writer is giving the offices, not a snapshot of one afternoon.

'Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend;'

An officer over the officers — a layer of administration that did not exist under David.

And two sons of Nathan in one verse. If this is the prophet who confronted David and then arranged the succession at Gihon, his family is now inside the government, and one of them holds the title Hushai held: king's friend.

'Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.'

There is the name to keep, at the bottom of the list where nobody looks.

Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.

That office appeared once before, in the last cabinet list in 2 Samuel, and it was new even then: Adoram was in charge of the forced labor (2 Sam. 20:24). Same post, and almost certainly the same man under a fuller form of his name.

Now follow him forward. Under Solomon the forced labour becomes enormous — chapter 5 has thirty thousand men conscripted in shifts, and seventy thousand burden-bearers, and eighty thousand quarrymen. And when Solomon dies, the northern tribes come to his son with exactly one request: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (12:4).

Rehoboam refuses, with the line about scorpions. And then: then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (12:18).

The man in this verse is stoned to death by the ten tribes eight chapters from now, and the kingdom splits over his department.

The writer puts him last on a list of eleven officials and says nothing whatever.

'Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year.'

Twelve districts, each responsible for feeding the court for one month.

It is an elegant arrangement, and look exactly at what it does. The burden is spread, so no region is ruined; the supply is continuous, so the court never runs short; and the whole country is now organised around the maintenance of the capital.

'These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan;'

'Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher); Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);'

'Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean which is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam;'

Now read the district list as a whole rather than name by name, because the shape of it is the information.

These are not the twelve tribes.

Some districts carry a tribal name — Naphtali, Asher, Issachar, Benjamin, Gilead. Others are defined by towns and regions that cut straight across the old inheritances: the hill country of Ephraim, Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh, Arubboth, Naphath-dor, Taanach and Megiddo and Beth-shean.

The tribal boundaries were not administrative conveniences. They were allotments, given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of the land God promised Abraham, and the law made them almost impossible to alienate permanently. A man's field was his tribe's and his tribe's was God's gift.

The new map is drawn over the top of them, for the purpose of collecting food.

It is more efficient. It is also the beginning of the dissolution of the thing that made Israel a covenant people rather than a country, and when the north finally walks out in chapter 12 the slogan they use is about inheritance: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse (12:16).

'Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars);'

'Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;'

Mahanaim is where David crossed the Jordan when Absalom drove him out, and where three men brought him beds and cheese.

'Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);'

'Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;'

Two of Solomon's daughters are married to district officers, and a son of Hushai holds a district. Hushai is the old man in the torn coat who walked into a captured Jerusalem and lied to Absalom's face to save David's life.

The families that stood by the father are being provided for by the son.

'Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar;'

'Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin;'

'Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.'

Twelve names, twelve districts, and one man over the whole system.

A reader who counts will notice something the writer does not mention: Judah is not on the list.

The Hebrew of the last verse is difficult and translations differ over whether a twelfth district in Judah is being referred to. What is not in doubt is that eleven of the districts named are in the north and centre, and that the tribe the king belongs to does not appear among them.

Whether Judah was exempt from the monthly provision, the text does not say outright. But the ten tribes will say something in chapter 12 that sounds very much as though they thought so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Every Man Under His Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy (v. 20). Solomon rules from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, and they bring tribute all his life (v. 21). The daily provision of his table is thirty cors of fine flour and sixty of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl (vv. 22-23). He has peace on every side (v. 24), and Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon (v. 25). Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen (v. 26), and the officers keep the supply coming without fail (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: As the sand by the sea is Abraham's promise arriving (Gen. 22:17), and the borders in verse 21 are the land as it was described to him (Gen. 15:18). This is the high-water mark of the whole Old Testament story, and the writer says so in that vocabulary on purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: And in the middle of it, forty thousand stalls of horses. The law said Israel's king must not acquire many horses (Deut. 17:16), and the reader has just watched his father hamstring seventeen hundred captured chariot horses on the day he won them, in obedience to that command (2 Sam. 8:4). The father cut the tendons. The son built the stables.

verseByVerse.quote: Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy. Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life. Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl. For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him. And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon. Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen. And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking. Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy.'

This is the high-water mark of the Old Testament, and the writer signals it with a phrase.

As many as the sand by the sea is not a general expression for a lot of people. It is the promise God swore to Abraham on the mountain in the land of Moriah, after the ram was found in the thicket: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen. 22:17).

Here it is, in a sentence about ordinary people eating dinner.

They ate and drank and were happy. That is the whole of it. Not conquering, not building, not fighting. Eating, drinking, and content.

'Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.'

The borders are Abraham's too. To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (Gen. 15:18).

Nothing before this and nothing after it comes as close. Joshua took the land; David subdued the neighbours; and here, for one generation, the map matches the promise.

'Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal,'

'ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.'

Per day.

A cor is something like six bushels, so this is several tons of flour and meal daily, thirty head of cattle, a hundred sheep, and game and poultry on top. Estimates of how many people that fed run into the thousands.

The passage is set down as splendour, and it is splendour, and it is also an invoice.

Somebody grew that grain and raised those animals, and the twelve districts of the previous paragraph exist precisely to deliver it, one month each. What reads as a description of the king's glory is, from the other end, a description of the country's tax burden — and the writer has put the two paragraphs in that order.

Hold both. The prosperity is real and the people are happy, and the machinery underneath it is what the north will complain about the day Solomon dies.

'For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him.'

He had peace on all sides around him.

His name means peace, and there is a reason he has it. God told David he would not build the temple because you have shed much blood and have waged great wars (1 Chron. 22:8), and promised instead a son who would be a man of rest.

This verse is that promise in operation. The wars were fought by the father so that the son could build.

'And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon.'

Here is the picture the prophets will use for the age to come.

Every man under his vine and under his fig tree.

It is a domestic image and that is its power. Not an empire, not a temple, not an army — a man sitting outside his own house in the shade of things he planted himself. A vine takes years to bear and a fig tree longer, so nobody sits under either unless he has been in one place long enough to plant them and safe enough to wait.

Micah takes it up for the day when the nations beat their swords into ploughshares: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid (Mic. 4:4). Zechariah uses it of the day God removes the iniquity of the land in a single day (Zech. 3:10).

So the settled prosperity of Solomon's reign becomes the standing Old Testament shorthand for what God intends to give the world, and notice what shape it takes. Peace, in Scripture, does not look like a throne. It looks like an ordinary person, unafraid, sitting in the shade of his own fig tree.

'Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen.'

Then this, in the middle of it, stated as one more item of glory.

The law about Israel's kings has three prohibitions, and the first is: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again" (Deut. 17:16).

Forty thousand stalls.

And the reader has watched somebody obey this command, recently and at cost. When David captured Hadadezer's cavalry he had almost all of the chariot horses hamstrung on the field, keeping enough for a hundred chariots and destroying the rest — the finest military asset in the region, deliberately ruined, because of one clause in a book (2 Sam. 8:4).

The father cut the tendons. The son built the stables.

And chapter 10 will complete it: Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt (10:28), which is the other half of the same prohibition, the half about sending people back where they came from.

The reason the law gives is never economic. It is that a chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and a psalm of David says so directly: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7).

The writer records the forty thousand stalls between a verse about men sitting under their fig trees and a verse about the officers never letting the supply fail, and he does not say one word about it.

'And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking.'

'Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.'

They let nothing be lacking. The system works perfectly, and the last verse of the section is about feeding the horses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — Wisdom Like the Sand on the Seashore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore (v. 29), surpassing all the east and all Egypt (v. 30). He is wiser than Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations (v. 31). He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005 (v. 32). He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish (v. 33). And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue in verse 33 runs the categories of Genesis 1. This wisdom is not mysticism and not a technique; it is sustained attention to what God has made, from the largest tree in the region to the weed in a wall.
verseByVerse.examples: Two of the men he is measured against — Ethan and Heman — have psalms in the psalter with their names in the headings (Pss. 88, 89). And the last verse points forward: people came from everywhere to hear him, and one of them arrives in chapter 10, and the Lord Jesus says of himself something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42).

verseByVerse.quote: And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore, so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations. He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005. He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish. And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore,'

The promise at Gibeon is being reported as fact, and the writer uses the same figure he used of the population two paragraphs ago: like the sand on the seashore.

Breadth of mind is literally largeness of heart. It is not a moral phrase here; it means range — the capacity to hold a great many things and see how they fit.

'so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.'

Those were the two great wisdom traditions of the ancient world, and the writer names them because his readers would have known the comparison was a real one. Egypt had centuries of instruction literature; the east had its own. Solomon is being placed above both.

'For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations.'

Four named men, evidently famous enough that no explanation was needed.

Two of them turn up in the psalter. Psalm 88 is a maskil of Heman the Ezrahite, and it is the darkest psalm in the book — the one that ends darkness is my closest friend. Psalm 89 is a maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite, and it is the long meditation on the covenant with David that asks, when the crown has been thrown to the ground, Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?

The men Solomon is measured against wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant. That is what wisdom was understood to be in Israel: not a stock of good advice, but the ability to look steadily at things that do not resolve.

'He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005.'

Three thousand proverbs, and the book of Proverbs contains a few hundred of his. A thousand and five songs, and the Song of Songs is one, and two psalms carry his name (Pss. 72, 127).

Almost all of it is lost. The writer records the numbers so that we understand what a small fraction survived.

'He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish.'

This is the verse that tells us what kind of thing his wisdom actually was.

Read the categories: trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, fish.

That is Genesis 1. It is the order of the created world as the first chapter of the Bible sets it out, and Solomon went through it and paid attention.

The range within the first category is the whole point: from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. The cedar is the largest and most valuable tree in the region, the timber kings imported for palaces and temples. Hyssop is a small bushy plant that grows in cracks in masonry, and it is what the Israelites used to daub blood on the doorposts in Egypt, and what was lifted to the cross with a sponge of sour wine.

The biggest tree and the weed in the wall. He looked at both.

So the wisdom God gave was not a mystical faculty or a stock of clever rulings. It was attention — sustained, curious, unembarrassed attention to what God had made, from the cedars down to whatever is growing out of the brickwork.

That is what the book of Proverbs does on every page. Go to the ant. Look at the badger and the locust and the lizard. Watch how a lazy man's field looks in the spring. Israel's wisdom tradition believed the world was made by a God who is consistent, and that a person who watches it carefully will learn how to live.

'And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.'

People came from everywhere, and one of them gets a chapter to herself.

The Queen of Sheba arrives in chapter 10, tests him with hard questions, and says the half was not told her.

And there is one more thing to say about this verse, because the Lord Jesus said it. Speaking to a generation that wanted a sign from him, he said: the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42).

A foreign queen crossed a desert on a rumour. And the people standing in front of the wisdom of God in person asked him to do a trick.

4.theology:
A state, not a court (vv. 2-6). Two secretaries, an officer set over the officers, a palace manager, and a department of forced labour — layers David never had. Note also two sons of Nathan inside the government, one of them holding the title Hushai held, king's friend; and Jehoshaphat the recorder, who has now served two kings.

The seed of the split, eleventh on the list (v. 6). The office was new when it first appeared at 2 Samuel 20:24. Under Solomon it becomes enormous — chapter 5 has thirty thousand conscripted in shifts, seventy thousand burden-bearers, eighty thousand quarrymen. And when he dies, the north asks Rehoboam for exactly one thing: lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke (12:4). He refuses, sends this man, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (12:18).

A revenue map over an inheritance (vv. 7-19). Some districts carry tribal names; others are defined by towns that cut across the old boundaries. Those boundaries were allotments given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of what was promised to Abraham, and the law made them nearly impossible to alienate permanently. Drawing a new map over them for the purpose of collecting food is efficient, and it begins dissolving the thing that made Israel a covenant people rather than a country — and the slogan the north eventually uses is about inheritance (12:16). A reader who counts will also notice that Judah does not appear among the districts named; the Hebrew of the last verse is difficult, and what is not in doubt is that the tribe the king belongs to is not on the list.

Abraham's promise arriving (vv. 20-21). As many as the sand by the sea is what God swore on the mountain in Moriah after the ram was found in the thicket (Gen. 22:17), and the borders in verse 21 are the land as described to him (Gen. 15:18). Nothing before this and nothing after comes as close. And the sentence it is put in is about ordinary people eating dinner: they ate and drank and were happy.

Splendour, and an invoice (vv. 22-23). Several tons of flour and meal a day, thirty head of cattle, a hundred sheep, and game and poultry besides. Somebody grew that and raised it, and the twelve districts exist to deliver it a month each. What reads from one end as the king's glory is from the other end the country's tax burden, and the writer put the paragraphs in that order. Hold both: the prosperity is real and the people are happy, and the machinery underneath is what the north complains about the day he dies.

Peace on all sides (v. 24). His name means peace, and there is a reason he has it. God told David he would not build the temple because you have shed much blood and have waged great wars, and promised instead a son who would be a man of rest (1 Chron. 22:8-9). The wars were fought by the father so the son could build.

What peace looks like in Scripture (v. 25). Not a throne, not an empire, not an army — a man sitting outside his own house in the shade of things he planted himself. A vine takes years to bear and a fig tree longer, so nobody sits under either unless he has been somewhere long enough to plant them and safe enough to wait. Micah takes it up for the day the nations beat their swords into ploughshares (Mic. 4:4), and Zechariah for the day God removes the iniquity of the land (Zech. 3:10). The settled prosperity of this reign becomes the standing shorthand for what God intends to give the world.

Forty thousand stalls (v. 26). The first of the three prohibitions on Israel's kings is he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses (Deut. 17:16) — and the reader has just watched somebody obey it at real cost, hamstringing the finest cavalry in the region on the day he captured it (2 Sam. 8:4). Chapter 10 completes the breach: Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt (10:28). The reason the law gives is never economic; a chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and a psalm of David says so: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7). The writer sets the forty thousand stalls between men under their fig trees and officers who let nothing be lacking, and says nothing.

Who he is measured against (v. 31). Two of the four turn up in the psalter. Psalm 88 is Heman's, the darkest psalm in the book, ending darkness is my closest friend. Psalm 89 is Ethan's, the long meditation on the covenant with David that asks, with the crown thrown to the ground, Lord, where is your steadfast love of old? The men Solomon surpasses wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant. That is what wisdom meant in Israel: not a stock of good advice but the capacity to look steadily at what does not resolve.

What his wisdom actually was (v. 33). Trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, fish — the categories of Genesis 1, gone through with attention. And the range inside the first one is the point: from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. The cedar is the timber kings imported for palaces; hyssop is a weed in masonry, and it is what daubed blood on the doorposts in Egypt and what lifted a sponge to the cross. The biggest tree and the plant in the brickwork, and he looked at both. That is what Proverbs does on every page — go to the ant, watch the badger and the locust and the lizard, look at a lazy man's field in spring. Israel's wisdom believed the world was made by a consistent God and that watching it carefully teaches you how to live. Note also how little survived: three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, of which we have a few hundred proverbs, one song, and two psalms.

Something greater (v. 34). People came from everywhere, and one of them gets a chapter to herself in chapter 10. And the Lord Jesus used this verse against a generation that wanted a sign from him: the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42). A foreign queen crossed a desert on a rumour; the people standing in front of the wisdom of God in person asked him to do a trick.
4.examples:
Then: A king whose court ate thirty head of cattle and a hundred sheep a day reorganised the whole country into twelve supply districts drawn straight across the tribal inheritances — and the minister he put in charge of the conscripted labour that built it all was stoned to death by ten of the tribes on the day the kingdom broke in half.

Now: Two things. Verse 33 is what wisdom looks like when the Bible describes it, and it is more ordinary and more demanding than most people expect: not a mystical faculty and not a stock of clever answers, but sustained attention to what God has actually made, from the cedars of Lebanon down to whatever is growing out of a wall. Solomon was the wisest man alive and he spent it looking at fish and lizards. And the second is the shape of the chapter. Everything in it is a genuine good — peace, plenty, safety, a man under his own fig tree, a promise to Abraham arriving — and the writer lays the machinery that pays for it right alongside, and drops forty thousand stalls of horses into the middle without a word. Prosperity is not neutral. It has a bill attached and somebody is carrying it, and it quietly acquires the things it was told not to.
